cards.label: §20.18 Derivation
cards.title: General ellipse from two perpendicular waves: eliminating t
cards.legend: Two plane waves travel along x, one vibrating along y and one along z, with amplitudes E_1 and E_2 and phase difference δ. φ stands for kx − ωt. On the right a phase circle of radius 1: its angle φ gives cos φ = E_y/E_1, and the angle φ + δ gives the second wave. Left: the path of the tip of E in the y–z plane, drawn here for E_1 = 55, E_2 = 40, δ = 60°, with the tilted major axis at angle α to the y-axis.

draw.caption: Light travels along x; E lies in the y–z plane
The tip of E traces a closed curve
E at one instant: E_y along y, E_z along z
Phase circle: angle φ and φ + δ

phases.name: Two waves
phases.why: write E_y and E_z for the two perpendicular waves

phases.name: Remove time
phases.why: expand cos(φ + δ), write cos φ and sin φ with E_y

phases.name: Clear the root
phases.why: isolate the root, square, and use cos² δ + sin² δ = 1

phases.name: Ellipse
phases.why: divide by E_2² to get the general ellipse equation

steps.note: Write the two waves with \(\phi = kx-\omega t\) (Eqs. 20.37, 20.38). The wave polarised along \(y\) has amplitude \(E_1\).
The wave polarised along \(z\) has amplitude \(E_2\) and is ahead by the phase difference \(\delta\).
Expand the cosine of a sum, \(\cos(\phi+\delta) = \cos\phi\cos\delta-\sin\phi\sin\delta\), so that \(E_z\) is written with \(\cos\phi\) and \(\sin\phi\) (Eq. 20.40).

ask.why: The cosine of a sum is the product of cosines minus the product of sines.

figure.caption: cos(φ + δ): angles φ and δ add

steps.note: From the first wave, \(E_y = E_1\cos\phi\). Divide by \(E_1\) to get \(\cos\phi\) alone, so that \(t\) can be eliminated.
In the right triangle on the phase circle the hypotenuse is 1, the leg next to \(\phi\) is \(\cos\phi\) and the leg opposite is \(\sin\phi\). Pythagoras gives \(\sin^2\phi+\cos^2\phi=1\).

ask.q: In the right triangle with hypotenuse 1 and angle \(\phi\), \(\sin^2\phi + \cos^2\phi\) equals
ask.why: The two legs are \(\cos\phi\) and \(\sin\phi\); the sum of their squares is the hypotenuse squared, 1.

figure.caption: △: hypotenuse 1, legs cos φ and sin φ

steps.note: Rearrange: move \(\cos^2\phi\) across and take the square root. The sign is either one, as the wave goes up or down.
Put \(\cos\phi = E_y/E_1\) inside the root.

figure.caption: Use cos φ = E_y/E_1 under the root

steps.note: Replace \(\cos\phi\) and \(\sin\phi\) in the expanded \(E_z\) (Eq. 20.41). Time now appears nowhere. (The two signs are written \(\pm\), as in the book.)

figure.caption: t is gone: E_z written with E_y only

steps.note: Move the \(\cos\delta\) term to the left so that the square root stands alone on the right.

figure.caption: Square root alone on the right

steps.note: Square both sides. This removes the root and the \(\pm\).

ask.q: Why do we square both sides?
options: To remove the square root and the ± sign
ask.why: The square of either sign is the same, and the square of a root is the quantity under it.

steps.note: Expand the square on the left and multiply out the bracket on the right.
Bring the \(\sin^2\delta\) term from the right to the left and collect the two \(E_y^2\) terms (Eq. 20.42).
The same right-triangle identity as before, now for the angle \(\delta\): hypotenuse 1, adjacent leg \(\cos\delta\), opposite leg \(\sin\delta\).

ask.why: It is again the hypotenuse squared, 1.

figure.caption: △: hypotenuse 1, legs cos δ and sin δ

steps.note: Replace the bracket by 1.

Divide every term by \(E_2^2\) (Eq. 20.43). This is the general equation of an ellipse: the tip of the resultant \(E\) traces an ellipse in the \(y\)–\(z\) plane, inside a box of sides \(2E_1\) and \(2E_2\).

ask.q: Equation (20.43) describes the path of the tip of \(E\) as a
ask.why: Its \(y^2\) and \(z^2\) terms are both positive with a cross term, which is an ellipse.

move.label: Tilt of the major axis (quoted by the book)

steps.note: The book also quotes the tilt of the major axis: it makes angle \(\alpha\) with the \(y\)-axis. The same ellipse equation gives this tilt; the book states it without a derivation.

figure.caption: Major axis tilted by α to the y-axis

cards.label: §20.18 Derivation
cards.title: Special cases δ = 0 and δ = π: plane-polarised light
cards.legend: Special cases of the ellipse equation: δ = 0 (waves in phase) and δ = π (opposite phase). The rectangle has sides 2E_1 along y and 2E_2 along z (E_1 = 60, E_2 = 40 here). For these phases the ellipse shrinks to a diagonal of the rectangle; θ is its angle with the y-axis.

draw.caption: Axes y and z; E_1 along y, E_2 along z

phases.name: In phase, δ = 0
phases.why: put cos δ = 1, sin δ = 0, factor the square and solve

phases.name: Opposite phase, δ = π
phases.why: put cos δ = −1, sin δ = 0 and repeat

steps.note: Start from the general ellipse equation (20.43) of the previous card.
In phase means \(\delta = 0\) or \(\pm 2m\pi\). Then \(\cos\delta = 1\) and \(\sin\delta = 0\) (Eq. 20.43 case 1).

ask.q: For \(\delta = 0\), the values of \(\cos\delta\) and \(\sin\delta\) are

steps.note: The left side has the form \(a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\) with \(a = E_y/E_1\) and \(b = E_z/E_2\), which is \((a-b)^2\).

ask.q: Which identity turns \(a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\) into a square?

steps.note: A square is zero only if the quantity is zero. Take the square root of both sides.
Move \(E_z/E_2\) across and multiply by \(E_2\) (Eq. 20.44). This is a straight line through the origin with slope \(E_2/E_1\): the diagonal of the box.

In the right triangle with legs \(E_1\) along \(y\) and \(E_2\) along \(z\), the angle \(\theta\) at the origin has opposite side \(E_2\) and adjacent side \(E_1\). So \(\tan\theta = E_2/E_1\), the slope of the line.

ask.q: In the right triangle with legs \(E_1\) (adjacent to \(\theta\)) and \(E_2\) (opposite), \(\tan\theta\) equals

figure.caption: △: θ at O; E_2 opposite, E_1 adjacent

steps.note: Take the inverse tangent. Two waves in phase give a plane-polarised wave whose vibration makes the angle \(\tan^{-1}(E_2/E_1)\) with the \(y\)-axis.

figure.caption: In phase: plane-polarised at angle θ

steps.note: Opposite phase means \(\delta = \pi\) or \(\pm(2m+1)\pi\). Then \(\cos\delta = -1\) and \(\sin\delta = 0\) (case 2), so the cross term changes sign.

figure.caption: δ = π (or ±(2m+1)π): cos δ = −1, sin δ = 0

steps.note: Take the square root of both sides.

Solve for \(E_z\) (Eq. 20.45). This is a straight line of slope \(-E_2/E_1\), the other diagonal of the box, making the angle \(\tan^{-1}(-E_2/E_1) = -\theta\) with the \(y\)-axis. Two waves in opposite phase also give a plane-polarised wave.

cards.label: §20.18 Derivation
cards.title: Special case δ = π/2: elliptical and circular polarisation
cards.legend: Quarter-wave phase difference δ = π/2 (or ±(2m+1)π/2) between the y- and z-vibrations, amplitudes E_1 (along y) and E_2 (along z); E_1 = 60, E_2 = 40 here. The ellipse has its axes along y and z. When E_1 = E_2 = E_0 the box becomes a square and the ellipse a circle of radius E_0 (drawn with E_0 = E_2).

phases.name: Ellipse, δ = π/2
phases.why: put cos δ = 0, sin δ = 1 in the ellipse equation

phases.name: Circle, E_1 = E_2
phases.why: set the amplitudes equal to get a circle

steps.note: Start from the general ellipse equation (20.43).
For \(\delta = \pi/2\) or \(\pm(2m+1)\pi/2\), \(\cos\delta = 0\) and \(\sin\delta = 1\). The cross term vanishes and the right side becomes 1 (Eq. 20.46).

ask.q: For \(\delta = \pi/2\), the values of \(\cos\delta\) and \(\sin\delta\) are

figure.caption: δ = π/2: cos δ = 0, sin δ = 1

steps.note: Where does the curve cross the \(y\)-axis? Put \(E_z = 0\): then \(E_y^2/E_1^2 = 1\).

ask.q: Where does the ellipse \(E_y^2/E_1^2+E_z^2/E_2^2=1\) cut the \(y\)-axis?

figure.caption: E_z = 0: the curve meets the y-axis at ±E_1

steps.note: Put \(E_y = 0\): then \(E_z^2/E_2^2 = 1\). The curve crosses the \(z\)-axis at \(\pm E_2\).

figure.caption: E_y = 0: the curve meets the z-axis at ±E_2

steps.note: The book's tilt formula \(\tan 2\alpha = 2E_1E_2\cos\delta/(E_1^2-E_2^2)\) also gives zero when \(\cos\delta = 0\), so \(\alpha = 0\). The major and minor axes coincide with the \(y\)- and \(z\)-axes: the light is elliptically polarised.

figure.caption: α = 0: ellipse axes lie along y and z

steps.note: Now take equal amplitudes and call each one \(E_0\), with \(\delta = \pi/2\) still.
Put \(E_1 = E_2 = E_0\) into the ellipse equation (20.46).
Multiply both sides by \(E_0^2\) (Eq. 20.47). This is a circle of radius \(E_0\), so the resultant light is circularly polarised.

ask.q: With \(\delta = \pi/2\) and \(E_1 = E_2 = E_0\) the path of \(E\) is
ask.why: \(E_y^2+E_z^2 = E_0^2\) is a circle: circularly polarised light.
